title: Trump Overrules ICE's Traffic Stop Suspension, Orders Agents to Resume Vehicle Stops
excerpt: The president reversed his own administration's pause on immigration traffic stops within 24 hours, saying agents cannot give up one of their most effective tools — even as protests mount over two fatal shootings
body:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday morning publicly overruled his own administration's decision to suspend most Immigration and Customs Enforcement traffic stops, ordering agents to resume one of their most controversial enforcement tactics barely a day after it was paused.

"We must be strong, tough, and smart, and we CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.'s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. He urged officers to be "judicious, fair and smart" and to return to their work.

The reversal came just 24 hours after ICE leadership had instructed officers nationwide to halt most vehicle stops — a decision triggered by back-to-back fatal shootings that left two men dead during immigration enforcement operations.

## Two Fatal Shootings in Six Days

On July 7, an ICE officer in Houston fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national, during a vehicle stop. The Department of Homeland Security initially claimed Araujo had "weaponized" his vehicle, but witnesses in the involved van dispute that account.

Six days later, on July 13, an ICE agent shot and killed Joan Sebastian Durán Guerrero, a 26-year-old Colombian man, in Biddeford, Maine, about 15 miles south of Portland. DHS said officers had been conducting an operation related to a final order of removal and that an officer "fearing for public safety" discharged his weapon.

Neither man was the intended target of the deportation operations that led to their deaths, DHS officials have acknowledged. No body camera footage exists from either incident, and federal authorities have offered no evidence that either man posed a lethal threat to agents or the public.

## A Pattern of Enforcement Deaths

The two killings bring to at least seven the number of people shot dead during immigration enforcement operations since January 2025, when Trump returned to office and launched his mass deportation campaign. The shootings have sparked protests in Maine, Houston, and Boston, with demonstrators demanding independent investigations and accountability.

ICE arrests in Maine have more than quadrupled since the beginning of June, surging to around 70 per day in early July, according to internal ICE data.

## The Whiplash

Trump's border czar, Tom Homan, had described the suspension as a "temporary pause" — not a policy change — and said it would allow for a "short-term review to make sure ICE agents are safe and doing the right thing."

But Trump's swift reversal undercut that framing. The president's Truth Social post made clear he views traffic stops as essential to his immigration crackdown and does not want any restrictions on the practice.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin had personally discussed the pause with Senator Susan Collins (R-Maine) after Monday's shooting, according to sources familiar with their conversations.

## Body Camera Deployment Pledged

In the wake of the shootings, DHS pledged to "rapidly" deploy body cameras to ICE officers nationally — an acknowledgment of the lack of video evidence in both fatal incidents. The absence of body cameras has been a persistent criticism of ICE operations, with advocates arguing that the lack of footage makes accountability nearly impossible.

The back-to-back deaths have reignited the broader debate over immigration enforcement tactics at a time when communities with large immigrant populations already feel under siege. Traffic stops are one of ICE's most common tools for making arrests, and suspending them — even briefly — would have significantly impacted the agency's enforcement capacity.

## What This Means for Immigrant Communities

For the millions of immigrants living in the United States, Trump's reversal signals that the aggressive enforcement posture will not only continue but intensify. Community advocates and immigration attorneys have warned that the resumption of traffic stops — without body cameras or clear use-of-force protocols — creates a climate of fear.

The Indian-American community and other immigrant groups, many of whom commute through areas with heightened ICE activity, face the reality that any traffic stop could become an immigration enforcement encounter, regardless of the occupants' legal status.

*Sources: Reuters, The Wall Street Journal, CNN, Associated Press*
